title: EUR 60,000 MT202 with no customer behind it, and the team paid it anyway
explain:
An MT202 for EUR 60,000 arrives at a bank.
The team treats it as cover for a customer payment and releases the funds.
There was no customer payment behind it at all.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT202 arrives, moving funds between banks
→ The team assumes it settles a named MT103
→ No linking reference is checked
→ EUR 60,000 of the bank's own funds is paid out to a customer

The assumption was:
"Every MT202 is a cover payment."

Why?

An MT202 COV exists to settle a specific MT103: it moves the funds for that customer payment and carries the reference that binds the two messages together. A plain MT202 is a bank's own transfer, moving proprietary funds between banks with no customer payment behind it. Both move money between banks, yet only the COV answers to a customer instruction.

Both move money ≠ Both answer to a customer.

That distinction is what trips people up.

BA Takeaway

Check the reference before treating any MT202 as cover.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT202 COV, bound to a named MT103
→ Plain MT202, the bank's own funds
→ Linking reference on the cover leg
→ Customer payment the cover answers to

The real requirement isn't "Did an MT202 arrive?"

It's "What evidence proves this MT202 is cover for a named customer payment, not the bank's own transfer?"

Have you seen a bank-to-bank transfer mistaken for a customer payment?
takeaway: Both move money between banks, yet only the COV answers to a customer instruction, and that distinction is what trips people up.

title: EUR 120,000 sent on an MT202, and the beneficiary never existed
explain:
A bank sends EUR 120,000 to another bank on an MT202.
The receiving bank asks: which customer is this for?
There is no customer. The MT202 was never a customer payment.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment instruction raised for a named beneficiary
→ The team sends an MT202 instead of an MT103
→ The receiving bank looks for a beneficiary and finds none
→ The payment sits unapplied while the customer waits

The assumption was:
"An MT202 can carry a customer payment."

Why?

An MT103 is a customer payment instruction: it orders the receiving bank to pay a named beneficiary a named amount. An MT202 is a bank-to-bank instruction that moves funds between banks with no customer beneficiary attached. Every customer payment starts with an MT103, and an MT202 appears only when a separate funds leg is required.

A funds movement ≠ A customer payment.

BA Takeaway

Start every customer payment with an MT103, and add an MT202 only for the funds leg.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Customer instruction (MT103) with named beneficiary
→ Bank-to-bank funds leg (MT202) where one is needed
→ Beneficiary the receiving bank can pay
→ Payment applied, not sitting unapplied

The real requirement isn't "Did we send the money?"

It's "What evidence proves the receiving bank got a customer instruction it could actually apply?"

Have you seen a customer payment sent on a message that has nowhere to name the customer?
takeaway: Every customer payment starts with an MT103, and an MT202 appears only when a separate funds leg is required.

title: EUR 35,000 credited to the wrong account because field 59 was never read
explain:
A EUR 35,000 payment arrives at a bank.
The operations team credits it using the account in the remittance text.
The real beneficiary, named in field 59, never receives it.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 arrives with field 59 naming the beneficiary and account
→ Field 57 names the beneficiary bank by BIC
→ The team reads the free-text remittance instead of field 59
→ The money is credited to the wrong account

The assumption was:
"The remittance text tells us who to pay."

Why?

Field 59 names the beneficiary customer and the account to be credited, so it is the first field to check when a payment must reach the right person. Field 57 names the beneficiary bank by BIC, telling the chain which bank must receive the instruction. In a serial payment each bank reads both fields from the MT103 it receives and forwards the message to the next bank in the chain.

Free text ≠ Field 59.

BA Takeaway

Read field 59 first, every time, before any credit is posted.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 59, beneficiary customer and account
→ Field 57, beneficiary bank by BIC
→ Free-text remittance, never the source of the payee
→ Credit posted only to the field 59 account

The real requirement isn't "Did we credit someone?"

It's "What evidence proves the credit went to the account named in field 59?"

Have you seen a payment credited to the wrong person because a free-text note was trusted over the field?
takeaway: In a serial payment each bank reads both fields from the MT103 it receives and forwards the message to the next bank in the chain.

title: EUR 80,000 screened against the wrong name, because field 50 was skipped
explain:
An EUR 80,000 payment is screened and cleared.
Days later, compliance finds the ordering customer was on a watchlist.
The screening had checked the name in field 72, not the ordering customer in field 50.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 arrives, field 50 naming the ordering customer
→ Field 72 carries extra sender-to-receiver information
→ Screening runs against a name pulled from field 72
→ The real ordering customer is never checked

The assumption was:
"Any name in the message is good enough for screening."

Why?

Field 50 identifies the ordering customer, the party who instructed the payment, and it is the first field screening and reconciliation check. Field 72 carries sender-to-receiver information, the extra instructions that fit no structured field. The two fields answer different questions: field 50 says who is paying, field 72 says what else the receiver needs to know.

Field 72 ≠ Field 50.

BA Takeaway

Screen the ordering customer in field 50 first, and treat field 72 as extra information only.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Field 50, who is paying
→ Field 72, what else the receiver needs to know
→ Screening run on the field 50 party
→ Reconciliation matched on the field 50 party

The real requirement isn't "Did we screen a name?"

It's "What evidence proves screening ran on the ordering customer in field 50?"

Have you seen a check pass because it ran on the wrong field?
takeaway: The two fields answer different questions: field 50 says who is paying, field 72 says what else the receiver needs to know.

title: EUR 4,000 refunded under SDD B2B, and the scheme said it could never happen
explain:
A business debtor claims a EUR 4,000 refund on a direct debit.
The bank pays it, no reason asked.
The creditor protests: this was an SDD B2B collection, and B2B grants no refund right.

Here's how that happens:

→ Collection set up as SDD B2B, business to business only
→ The debtor claims a refund within eight weeks
→ The bank applies the SDD Core rule and refunds it
→ The creditor points out the scheme was B2B, not Core

The assumption was:
"All SEPA direct debits give an eight-week refund."

Why?

SDD Core covers collections from consumers and businesses, and it gives the debtor an eight-week refund right with no reason required. SDD B2B is restricted to business-to-business collections and grants no such refund right, which is why the debtor bank must verify the mandate before the first collection. The schemes differ on refunds and mandate checks.

Core ≠ B2B.

Using the wrong scheme is a real error, not a paperwork slip.

BA Takeaway

Verify the scheme and the mandate before the first collection, and apply that scheme's refund rule.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Scheme used: Core or B2B
→ Mandate verified before the first collection
→ Refund right that scheme actually grants
→ Refund decision made on the right scheme

The real requirement isn't "Did the debtor ask within eight weeks?"

It's "What evidence proves we applied the refund rule of the scheme this collection actually ran under?"

Have you seen a refund paid that the scheme never allowed?
takeaway: The schemes differ on refunds and mandate checks, so using the wrong one is a real error, not a paperwork slip.

title: EUR 25,000 SEPA payment rejected for the wrong reason code
explain:
A EUR 25,000 SEPA payment is rejected.
The team fixes the message format and resends it.
It is rejected again, with the same reason code.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment initiated with a pain.001
→ The scheme rejects it for a timing breach
→ The team rebuilds the message in a different format
→ The scheme rejects it again: the rule, not the format, was the problem

The assumption was:
"The format is the payment."

Why?

A SEPA payment is defined by scheme rules on timing, reason codes and returns, not by the message format that happens to carry it. The format is only the envelope: the same payment can be initiated with an MT101 or an MT103 as well as with a pain.001. That is why an MT103 and a pacs.008 can carry one underlying SEPA payment, the pacs.008 being its ISO 20022 form.

A new envelope ≠ A fixed payment.

BA Takeaway

Fix the scheme rule that failed, not the format that carried it.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Scheme rules: timing, reason codes, returns
→ Format carrying the payment
→ Reason code on the rejection
→ Fix applied to the rule that failed

The real requirement isn't "Did we resend it in a new format?"

It's "What evidence proves we fixed the scheme rule named in the reason code?"

Have you seen a payment resubmitted in a new format and rejected for the same rule?
takeaway: That is why an MT103 and a pacs.008 can carry one underlying SEPA payment, the pacs.008 being its ISO 20022 form.

title: EUR 45,000 MT103 arrived, and the team could not read it in MX
explain:
A EUR 45,000 payment arrives as an MT103.
The bank's new ISO 20022 platform cannot map it.
The team treats it as a new kind of payment and builds a new process for it.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 received, customer credit transfer
→ Platform expects pacs.008 and finds no mapping
→ The team builds a separate MT handling process
→ Two processes now do the same job, and returns fall between them

The assumption was:
"MT and MX are different payments."

Why?

A pacs.008 is the ISO 20022 customer credit transfer, the equivalent of an MT103, and a pacs.009 is the financial institution credit transfer, the equivalent of an MT202. A pacs.004 is the payment return, used when a pacs.008 cannot be applied and the funds must go back. The two families describe the same payments.

Same legs, new names.

A team moving from MT to MX only has to learn the new names for the same legs.

BA Takeaway

Map MT to MX by the leg, not by building a second process.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Customer leg: MT103, pacs.008
→ Bank leg: MT202, pacs.009
→ Return leg: pacs.004
→ One process handling both families

The real requirement isn't "Did we build an MX process?"

It's "What evidence proves every MT leg has an MX twin in the same process?"

Have you seen two processes doing one job because nobody mapped the names?
takeaway: The two families describe the same payments, so a team moving from MT to MX only has to learn the new names for the same legs.

title: EUR 200,000 MT103 sent by a corporate, and the chain rejected it
explain:
A corporate with its own BIC sends an MT103 for EUR 200,000 direct to a clearer.
The clearer rejects it.
The corporate's payment never enters the chain.

Here's how that happens:

→ Corporate instructs with an MT103, not an MT101
→ The clearer expects an instruction from a bank, not a corporate
→ The message is rejected at the first hop
→ The supplier waits while the corporate argues it has a BIC

The assumption was:
"A BIC of our own means we can send an MT103."

Why?

A corporation connected to SWIFT instructs its bank with an MT101, and it is the bank that sends the MT103, or the MT103 plus an MT202 COV, into the interbank chain. Even a corporate with its own BIC and a direct relationship with a clearer does not send an MT103 itself.

Corporates instruct, banks pay.

A BIC ≠ A banking licence to pay.

BA Takeaway

Route every corporate instruction through the bank, as an MT101, and let the bank issue the MT103.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Corporate instruction (MT101)
→ Bank payment into the chain (MT103, plus MT202 COV where needed)
→ Clearer relationship held by the bank
→ Payment actually entering the chain

The real requirement isn't "Does the corporate have a BIC?"

It's "What evidence proves the instruction reached the chain as a bank-issued MT103?"

Have you seen a corporate payment rejected because it skipped its own bank?
takeaway: The rule is simple: corporates instruct, banks pay.

title: USD 500,000 nostro debited twice, because two banks read one account
explain:
A bank holds USD 500,000 in a nostro account with another bank.
Both banks debit the same account for the same payment.
The account goes short, and neither bank can say why.

Here's how that happens:

→ Bank A holds a USD nostro with Bank B
→ Bank B calls the same account a vostro
→ A payment is debited from the nostro side
→ The same payment is debited again from the vostro side

The assumption was:
"Nostro and vostro are two different accounts."

Why?

When a bank holds an account with another bank in a foreign currency, it calls that account a nostro account, meaning our account with you. The bank that holds the account calls the very same account a vostro account, meaning your account with us. There is only one account, and the two words simply say which side of it each bank is standing on.

One account, two names.

BA Takeaway

Reconcile the single account from both sides, and never debit it twice for one payment.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Nostro view: our account with you
→ Vostro view: your account with us
→ Single balance both sides must agree on
→ One debit per payment, on the one account

The real requirement isn't "Did we debit the nostro?"

It's "What evidence proves both sides agree this is one account with one debit?"

Have you seen one account debited twice because two names made it look like two?
takeaway: There is only one account, and the two words simply say which side of it each bank is standing on.

title: EUR 70,000 payment read backwards, because nobody knew whose copy it was
explain:
An operations team investigates a EUR 70,000 payment.
The stored message says it is an output message.
The team concludes the bank received it.
The bank had actually sent it.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 stored in the archive with block 2
→ Team reads block 2 as an output message
→ They conclude the payment came into the bank
→ The real direction was the opposite: the bank sent it out

The assumption was:
"Block 2 means the same thing on every copy."

Why?

Block 2 of a SWIFT message, the application header, says whether the message is entering or leaving the SWIFT network. The same payment looks different from the two sides: from the sending bank it is an input message, and from the receiving bank it is an output message.

Input or output depends on your side.

An operator reading a stored message must therefore know which bank's copy it is looking at before deciding what block 2 means.

BA Takeaway

Identify whose copy you hold before reading block 2.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Bank whose copy is in hand
→ Direction from that bank's side
→ Block 2 read against that side
→ Conclusion about where the payment went

The real requirement isn't "What does block 2 say?"

It's "What evidence proves we know whose copy this is before we decide the direction?"

Have you seen an investigation go backwards because the wrong copy was read?
takeaway: An operator reading a stored message must therefore know which bank's copy it is looking at before deciding what block 2 means.

title: EUR 150,000 for two suppliers, squeezed into one MT103
explain:
A corporate must pay two suppliers EUR 150,000 in total.
It sends one MT103 naming both.
The second supplier is never paid, and the first is paid the full amount.

Here's how that happens:

→ One MT103 raised for a seller and a manufacturer
→ Field 59 carries a single beneficiary
→ The second beneficiary has nowhere to go in the message
→ The full amount is credited to the first supplier only

The assumption was:
"One message can pay two people."

Why?

An MT103 carries a single beneficiary in field 59, so one message pays one beneficiary at one bank. A payment that must reach a seller and a manufacturer at different banks needs two separate MT103 messages, one for each beneficiary.

One MT103, one beneficiary.

Trying to name two beneficiaries in a single MT103 is not possible, because the message has nowhere to put the second one.

BA Takeaway

Split every multi-beneficiary payment into one MT103 per beneficiary before sending.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Beneficiary one, with its own MT103
→ Beneficiary two, with its own MT103
→ Amount split per beneficiary
→ Credit confirmed per beneficiary

The real requirement isn't "Did we send the money?"

It's "What evidence proves every beneficiary got their own MT103 for their own amount?"

Have you seen a supplier unpaid because two payees were squeezed into one message?
takeaway: Trying to name two beneficiaries in a single MT103 is not possible, because the message has nowhere to put the second one.

title: EUR 55,000 valued a day late, because field 32A was read as the send date
explain:
A EUR 55,000 payment is sent on a Monday.
The receiving bank makes the funds available on Wednesday.
The beneficiary complains the value date was wrong, and the bank cannot explain it.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 sent on Monday, field 32A carrying a Wednesday value date
→ The team reads the send date as the value date
→ The beneficiary is told the funds are available Monday
→ The funds are actually available Wednesday, per field 32A

The assumption was:
"The value date is the date the message was sent."

Why?

Field 32A carries three things: the value date in year-month-day order, the currency, and the interbank settlement amount. The value date is the date the funds are to be available to the receiver, not the date the message was sent. The currency in field 32A is the currency the receiver's bank actually receives, which is why it can differ from the currency the ordering customer instructed in field 33B.

Send date ≠ Value date.

BA Takeaway

Read the value date, currency and settlement amount from field 32A, and tell the beneficiary the field 32A date.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Value date in field 32A
→ Currency the receiver actually gets
→ Interbank settlement amount
→ Currency instructed in field 33B, which can differ

The real requirement isn't "When did we send it?"

It's "What evidence proves the beneficiary was told the field 32A value date, not the send date?"

Have you seen a beneficiary promised funds on a date the field never said?
takeaway: The currency in field 32A is the currency the receiver's bank actually receives, which is why it can differ from the currency the ordering customer instructed in field 33B.

title: EUR 30,000 payment rejected because the name had one wrong character
explain:
A EUR 30,000 payment names a beneficiary with characters from their own script.
The SWIFT network rejects the message outright.
The beneficiary waits while the name is rewritten.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT103 raised with the beneficiary name in local script
→ The message enters the SWIFT network
→ The network rejects it: the characters are outside the allowed set
→ The payment never leaves the sending bank

The assumption was:
"A name is a name, in any script."

Why?

SWIFT MT messages use a restricted character set, and characters outside it cannot be used in a message at all. That is why country-specific characters, such as Japanese or Thai script, cannot appear in an MT101 or an MT103, even when the underlying instruction is domestic.

Names and addresses must be written with the characters the SWIFT set allows, or the message will not be accepted.

A name in the wrong script ≠ A valid message.

BA Takeaway

Validate every name and address against the SWIFT character set before the message is sent.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Name as the customer writes it
→ Name as the SWIFT set allows it
→ Validation before sending
→ Rejection handled before the beneficiary waits

The real requirement isn't "Did we spell the name right?"

It's "What evidence proves every character in the message is inside the SWIFT set?"

Have you seen a payment rejected for a single character the network would not accept?
takeaway: Names and addresses must be written with the characters the SWIFT set allows, or the message will not be accepted.

title: One MT101, three transfers, and the team built three processes
explain:
A corporate uses an MT101 to move EUR 40,000 between its own accounts.
It uses the same message to pay a domestic supplier EUR 25,000.
It uses it again to pay an overseas supplier EUR 60,000.
The bank built three separate processes for the same message.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT101 received for an own-account transfer
→ MT101 received for a domestic third-party payment
→ MT101 received for an international third-party payment
→ Three teams each build their own handling, and one fails

The assumption was:
"Different beneficiaries need different messages."

Why?

An MT101 can move funds between an ordering customer's own accounts, in favour of a third party domestically, and in favour of a third party internationally. All three uses are valid, because the message is a general request for transfer, not a payment for one kind of beneficiary.

One message, three uses.

The same message therefore serves a corporate moving money between its own accounts and a corporate paying a supplier abroad.

BA Takeaway

Handle the MT101 once, as a general request for transfer, whatever the beneficiary.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Own-account transfer on MT101
→ Domestic third-party payment on MT101
→ International third-party payment on MT101
→ One handling process for all three

The real requirement isn't "Which kind of transfer is this?"

It's "What evidence proves all three uses of the MT101 run through the same tested process?"

Have you seen three processes built for one message that does three jobs?
takeaway: The same message therefore serves a corporate moving money between its own accounts and a corporate paying a supplier abroad.

title: EUR 300,000 of advices, and the day-end statement disagreed
explain:
A corporate receives MT900 and MT910 advices all day for EUR 300,000 of movements.
At day end the MT950 statement arrives.
The statement total does not match the advices.

Here's how that happens:

→ MT900 and MT910 advices arrive as each debit and credit lands
→ The owner tracks every movement as it happens
→ The MT950 gathers all the movements into one statement
→ One movement is on the advices but missing from the statement

The assumption was:
"The statement is always right, so the advices can be ignored."

Why?

Through the day a bank sends MT900 and MT910 advices as each debit and credit lands on the account, so the owner hears about every movement as it happens. At day end the MT950 arrives and gathers all those movements into a single statement. The two must reconcile, since the advices and the statement describe the same day from different angles.

Advices ≠ Statement, until they reconcile.

BA Takeaway

Reconcile the advices against the MT950 every day, and chase every difference.

Keep these controls separate:

→ MT900 debit advices through the day
→ MT910 credit advices through the day
→ MT950 statement at day end
→ Reconciliation of the two views

The real requirement isn't "Did the statement arrive?"

It's "What evidence proves every advice is on the statement, and every difference was chased?"

Have you seen a day-end statement disagree with the advices that described the same day?
takeaway: The two must reconcile, since the advices and the statement describe the same day from different angles.

title: EUR 95,000 'confirmed' by instruction, but the credit never landed
explain:
A corporate is told EUR 95,000 is on its way.
It treats the funds as received and releases goods.
The credit never lands, because the instruction was never a posting.

Here's how that happens:

→ Payment instruction sent toward the account
→ The corporate treats the instruction as proof of receipt
→ No MT910 arrives, because no credit was ever posted
→ The goods are gone and the money never arrived

The assumption was:
"An instruction to pay is proof the money arrived."

Why?

The MT910 goes from the account servicing bank to the account owner as confirmation that a credit has been posted. It is triggered by the credit entry itself, so it follows real posting rather than a mere instruction to pay. On receipt, the owner can treat the funds as received, with certainty that the account was credited.

An instruction ≠ A posting.

BA Takeaway

Treat funds as received only on the MT910, never on the instruction.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Instruction to pay, sent
→ Credit entry posted on the account
→ MT910 confirmation of the posting
→ Goods or funds released on receipt

The real requirement isn't "Was the payment instructed?"

It's "What evidence proves the credit was actually posted before anything was released on it?"

Have you seen goods released on an instruction that never became a credit?
takeaway: On receipt, the owner can treat the funds as received, with certainty that the account was credited.

title: USD 250,000 in the mirror, and zero in the real nostro
explain:
A bank needs USD 250,000 from its nostro account.
Its own books, the mirror nostro, show USD 250,000 available.
The real account at the other bank shows zero.

Here's how that happens:

→ Bank A opens a USD account with Bank B, its nostro
→ Bank A keeps a mirror nostro in its own books
→ The mirror shows USD 250,000 expected
→ The real account at Bank B was never funded

The assumption was:
"The mirror holds the money."

Why?

When Bank A opens an account with Bank B, that account is Bank A's nostro, held in Bank B's books, and the real funds sit there. Bank A also keeps a mirror nostro in its own books, but the mirror holds no funds; it only reflects activity on the real account. The mirror is kept in the real account's currency, so a USD nostro carries a USD mirror, and the mirror lets a bank work out what the real account should show.

Mirror ≠ Money.

BA Takeaway

Fund and check the real nostro, and use the mirror only to work out what it should show.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Real nostro at the other bank, where funds sit
→ Mirror nostro in our own books, holding no funds
→ Currency matched on both sides
→ Real balance checked before any payment is promised

The real requirement isn't "What does the mirror show?"

It's "What evidence proves the real account at the other bank holds the funds?"

Have you seen a payment promised on a mirror balance that the real account never had?
takeaway: The mirror is kept in the real account's currency, so a USD nostro carries a USD mirror, and the mirror lets a bank work out what the real account should show.

title: EUR 8,000 sent 'on SWIFT' inside one country, and it never arrived
explain:
A customer sends EUR 8,000 to another account in the same country.
The sending bank routes it on SWIFT.
The payment never arrives, because the domestic system never sees it.

Here's how that happens:

→ Domestic payment raised inside one country
→ The team sends it through the SWIFT network
→ The domestic clearing system never receives it
→ The beneficiary waits while the payment sits in the wrong network

The assumption was:
"SWIFT carries every payment."

Why?

A payment inside one country runs through that country's own clearing and settlement systems, in local formats built on flat or XML files, and never touches the SWIFT network. SWIFT was created for cross-border payments, and the large majority of those still travel on it.

Local networks carry local payments and SWIFT carries payments that cross a border; the two worlds stay separate.

A domestic payment on SWIFT ≠ A payment on its way.

BA Takeaway

Route domestic payments through the domestic system, and SWIFT only across a border.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Payment inside one country, local clearing
→ Payment across a border, SWIFT
→ Local format used for the domestic leg
→ Beneficiary reached on the right network

The real requirement isn't "Did we send it?"

It's "What evidence proves the payment travelled on the network built for its journey?"

Have you seen a domestic payment lost in a network it never belonged on?
takeaway: Local networks carry local payments and SWIFT carries payments that cross a border; the two worlds stay separate.

title: EUR 100,000 of currency bought at the wrong price, because bid and ask were read backwards
explain:
A customer sells EUR 100,000 of foreign currency to the bank.
They expect the higher price they saw quoted.
They receive the lower one, and the bank keeps the difference.

Here's how that happens:

→ Bank quotes a bid price and an ask price
→ The customer reads the ask as the price they will get
→ The bank buys from the customer at the bid, the lower price
→ The customer loses the spread they never knew existed

The assumption was:
"Bid and ask are the same from both sides."

Why?

Bid means buy and ask means sell, and the bank sets both prices, not the customer. The bank buys currency from the customer at the bid rate and sells it to the customer at the ask rate, so the customer buys at the higher ask and sells at the lower bid, and the bank keeps the difference. A base currency exporter therefore watches the ask price, while a base currency importer watches the bid price.

The customer's buy ≠ The bank's buy.

Always read bid and ask from the bank's side.

BA Takeaway

Quote and check every FX price from the bank's side, and show the customer which side they are on.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Bid: the bank buys, the customer sells low
→ Ask: the bank sells, the customer buys high
→ Exporter watches the ask
→ Importer watches the bid

The real requirement isn't "Did we quote a price?"

It's "What evidence proves the customer was shown the price from their side of the trade?"

Have you seen a customer lose the spread because the prices were read from the wrong side?
takeaway: A base currency exporter therefore watches the ask price, while a base currency importer watches the bid price.

title: EUR 50,000 quoted the wrong way round, and the deal was priced in the wrong currency
explain:
A euro area bank quotes EUR/USD for a EUR 50,000 deal.
The dealer prices the deal in dollars.
The customer is charged in the wrong currency, and the deal has to be rebooked.

Here's how that happens:

→ Bank in the euro area quotes EUR/USD
→ The dealer treats the dollar as the price currency
→ The deal is priced in USD instead of EUR
→ The customer is charged in the wrong currency

The assumption was:
"Quoted and price currency are different things."

Why?

In a direct quote, the quoted currency is the domestic one, and quoted and price currency mean the same thing. For a bank in the euro area quoting EUR/USD, the euro is therefore the domestic currency and the price is expressed in euros. Keeping this the right way round matters, because the direct and indirect quotes describe the same pair from opposite sides.

Direct ≠ Indirect.

BA Takeaway

Price every direct quote in the domestic currency, and check the side before the deal is booked.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Domestic currency of the quoting bank
→ Quoted currency, the same as the price currency
→ Direct quote, price in domestic currency
→ Indirect quote, the same pair from the opposite side

The real requirement isn't "Did we quote the pair?"

It's "What evidence proves the deal was priced in the domestic currency of the quoting bank?"

Have you seen a deal rebooked because the quote was read from the wrong side?
takeaway: Keeping this the right way round matters, because the direct and indirect quotes describe the same pair from opposite sides.

title: Dealer buys EUR/USD, expects dollars, gets euros
explain:
A dealer buys EUR/USD for EUR 500,000.
The quote is 1.1635.
He expects USD 500,000 to land in the account.
Instead EUR 500,000 arrives, and USD 581,750 leaves it.

Here is how that happens:

→ Order placed: buy EUR/USD 500,000
→ EUR is the base currency, USD is the quoted currency
→ Buying means receiving EUR and paying USD
→ EUR 500,000 received, USD 581,750 paid at 1.1635

The assumption was:
"Buy EUR/USD means buy dollars."

It does not. Every buy or sell in a currency pair refers to the base currency, the first one named.

Why?

The quote number 1.1635 only states how much quoted currency one unit of base is worth. It says nothing about which currency changes hands. The trader read the pair backwards and booked the wrong side of the deal.

Buy EUR/USD means buy EUR, not USD.

Why does the pair name decide what you actually receive?

BA Takeaway

In EUR/USD, EUR is the base and USD is the quote, and every instruction refers to the base.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Base currency, what you buy or sell
→ Quoted currency, what you pay or receive
→ Quote number, the price of one unit of base

Show the base currency, the amount in base, and the amount in quoted currency on every deal ticket before it is confirmed.

The real requirement is not "What is the rate?"

It is "What evidence proves the dealer knows which currency is being bought?"

Have you seen a deal booked the wrong way round because the pair was read backwards?
takeaway: Every buy or sell in EUR/USD refers to EUR, the base currency, never to USD.

title: Merchant pays per card sale, holder pays nothing per sale
explain:
A shop takes EUR 10,000 in card sales in a week.
The owner expects the cardholders to carry the cost.
Instead his own statement shows a charge on every single sale.
The cardholders paid nothing per transaction.

Here is how that happens:

→ Customer pays EUR 100 by card
→ Merchant is charged by the issuer and the processing chain
→ Cardholder pays nothing for that transaction
→ Cardholder pays only the annual fee, plus interest if the balance is unpaid

The assumption was:
"The person who pays by card pays for the card payment."

The split works the other way round. The merchant pays per deal. The holder pays for holding the card.

Why?

A card transaction has two different bills. The merchant funds the acceptance chain on every sale, while the holder funds the card itself through the annual fee and through interest when a statement balance is not paid in full.

The merchant pays per deal. The holder pays per year.

Why does the same EUR 100 sale cost the merchant money and the holder nothing?

BA Takeaway

Who pays what on a card deal is fixed by role, not by who taps the card.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Merchant charges, per transaction accepted
→ Holder annual fee, for holding the card
→ Holder interest, only when a balance is unpaid

Show the merchant fee per transaction and the holder fee per year on separate lines, never as one blended card cost.

The real requirement is not "What does a card payment cost?"

It is "What evidence proves each side sees only the cost it actually bears?"

Have you seen a merchant surprised by the charge on a card sale they thought was free?
takeaway: The merchant pays per card sale. The holder pays nothing per transaction, only the annual fee and interest on an unpaid balance.

title: Monthly fee stays flat, processing fee follows every sale
explain:
A merchant pays EUR 200 a month to a processor.
In a quiet month he still pays EUR 200.
In a busy month the bill jumps to EUR 1,400.
He complains the monthly fee has gone up. It has not.

Here is how that happens:

→ Monthly fee charged: EUR 200, fixed every month
→ Processing fee charged: per transaction
→ Quiet month, few transactions, processing fee small
→ Busy month, many transactions, processing fee large

The assumption was:
"One fee to the processor, so one bill that moves together."

There are two fees, and they move on different rules. The monthly fee is fixed for using the service. The processing fee rises and falls with volume.

Why?

The processor charges for access and for use. Access is the monthly fee, set by the processing firm and the same every month. Use is the per-transaction fee, so a busy month costs more even though the monthly fee never changed.

A fixed fee and a volume fee are not the same bill.

Why does the bill jump in a busy month when the monthly fee never moves?

BA Takeaway

Separate the fee for access from the fee for use, or every busy month looks like a price rise.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Monthly fee, fixed for the processing service
→ Processing fee, per transaction, driven by volume
→ Total bill, the sum of the two, never one blended line

Show both fees on the statement, with the transaction count beside the processing fee.

The real requirement is not "What is the processor fee?"

It is "What evidence proves the merchant can see which part of the bill is fixed and which part follows volume?"

Have you seen a fixed fee blamed for a bill that really grew with volume?
takeaway: The monthly fee is fixed. The processing fee is per transaction, so it rises and falls with volume.

title: Cheque for EUR 25,000 clears, the paper never arrives
explain:
A customer deposits a cheque for EUR 25,000.
The paper cheque is lost in the post on its way to the paying bank.
The money still clears.
The branch had expected the paper to be essential. It was not.

Here is how that happens:

→ Beneficiary bank receives the cheque for EUR 25,000
→ Beneficiary bank presents an image of the cheque to the drawee bank
→ Drawee bank collects the funds from the image
→ No physical paper ever travels between the banks

The assumption was:
"A cheque must travel as paper to be collected."

In many countries it no longer has to. The beneficiary bank presents only an image, and clearing runs on the image.

Why?

Cheque clearing moved from moving paper to moving images. Once the image is accepted as the presentment, the physical journey adds nothing, and losing the paper no longer stops the collection.

The image is the presentment, not the paper.

Why does a lost paper cheque still clear when the image arrives safely?

BA Takeaway

Clearing follows the presentment the scheme accepts, and in many countries that presentment is an image.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Image captured, the presentment itself
→ Paper handling, storage and transport of the original
→ Funds collected, proved by the clearing response

Record the image presentment and the clearing result, not the paper journey, as the proof the cheque cleared.

The real requirement is not "Where is the paper cheque?"

It is "What evidence proves the cheque was presented and the funds were collected?"

Have you seen a cheque clear from an image while the paper was still missing?
takeaway: Cheque clearing now runs on images, not on the movement of paper.

title: File accepted, EUR 120,000 supplier still unpaid
explain:
A company sends a supplier file for EUR 120,000.
The bank replies: file accepted.
Finance tells the supplier the money is on its way.
Three days later the supplier says nothing arrived.

Here is how that happens:

→ pain.001 file sent, EUR 120,000 to suppliers
→ File acknowledgement received, receipt only
→ Validation passes, but clearing rejects two suppliers
→ Settlement never happens for those two, and no one notices

The requirement said:
"If the file is accepted, every supplier is paid."

Acceptance is only receipt. A payment is seven stages, and the file acknowledgement covers the first one.

Why?

Each stage has its own owner, status and failure mode: initiation, validation, processing, routing, clearing, settlement and confirmation. A rejection at clearing stays hidden when the team reads acceptance as settlement, so the failure only surfaces when the supplier complains.

File accepted is not money paid.

Why does a clean acknowledgement hide two unpaid suppliers for three days?

BA Takeaway

Diagnose by stage and evidence, never by the first status that looks good.

Keep these controls separate:

→ File receipt, the acknowledgement only
→ Clearing result, accepted or rejected per supplier
→ Settlement and confirmation, proved per payment

Show the status of every supplier at every stage, and alert on any clearing rejection the same day.

The real requirement is not "Was the file accepted?"

It is "What evidence proves each supplier was settled and confirmed?"

Have you seen a file acknowledgement treated as proof of payment?
takeaway: File accepted means receipt only. A payment is seven stages, and mistaking acceptance for settlement hides failures.

title: Migration team changes the network, the messages stay broken
explain:
A bank starts an ISO 20022 migration for a EUR 50,000 payment flow.
The team plans a network change.
Months later the messages still fail validation.
The network was never the problem.

Here is how that happens:

→ Payment travels over SWIFT as MT messages
→ Team scopes a network change, SWIFT to something new
→ Message content stays in the old MT format
→ Validation still fails, because the content never changed

The assumption was:
"SWIFT and ISO 20022 are the same thing, so changing one fixes the other."

They are different things. SWIFT is the network and service carrying messages between banks. ISO 20022 is the standard defining what those messages contain.

Why?

The same payment can travel over SWIFT as older MT or newer MX messages, and changing the standard changes nothing about the network. The migration is about message content, mapping and validation, not about a network change, so a network plan leaves the real work untouched.

Carrier is not content.

Why does a network change leave the same messages failing validation?

BA Takeaway

Scope the migration to what actually changes: content, mapping and validation.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Network, who carries the message
→ Standard, what the message contains
→ Mapping and validation, how old content becomes new

Write the scope as message content first, and name the network only where it truly changes.

The real requirement is not "Which network do we move to?"

It is "What evidence proves each message maps and validates under the new standard?"

Have you seen a migration scoped as a network change when the messages were the real work?
takeaway: SWIFT is the network. ISO 20022 is the standard. Changing one changes nothing about the other.

title: First collection for EUR 850 rejected, mandate was never set up
explain:
A creditor sends its first collection for EUR 850 under a new mandate.
The file is built, checked and sent.
The scheme rejects it the same day.
The mandate was never set up.

Here is how that happens:

→ Mandate signed by the debtor
→ Collection file built for EUR 850
→ Mandate setup check skipped, file sent first
→ Scheme rejects the first collection, no mandate on record

The requirement said:
"Build the file, then check the mandate."

That order is backwards. A collection cannot run before its mandate is set up and its authorisation evidence is in place.

Why?

Creditor and debtor roles must be unambiguous, mandate data complete, and the same mandate reference carried through every downstream system the scheme will see. A first collection on an incomplete mandate is rejected, so the setup check belongs before the file is built, not after the rejection lands.

No mandate, no collection.

Why does a signed mandate still fail when the setup check runs after the file is built?

BA Takeaway

Put the setup check before the file, and carry one mandate reference through every system.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Mandate setup, complete and evidenced
→ Mandate reference, the same in every system
→ First collection, only after setup is proved

Block file build until mandate setup passes, and show the mandate reference on the collection.

The real requirement is not "Was the file sent?"

It is "What evidence proves the mandate is set up before the first collection?"

Have you seen a first collection rejected because the mandate setup was checked too late?
takeaway: A first collection on an incomplete mandate is rejected, so put the setup check before the file is built.

title: Same debtor, same EUR 850, wrong sequence, collection fails
explain:
A creditor collects EUR 850 from the same debtor every month.
This month the collection is marked recurring.
The debtor bank treats it under the wrong rules and it fails.
It was the first collection under a new mandate.

Here is how that happens:

→ New mandate signed, first collection due for EUR 850
→ Collection marked recurring, copied from last month
→ Debtor bank applies recurring rules to a first collection
→ Collection fails under the wrong sequence

The assumption was:
"Same amount, same debtor, so the same sequence."

First and recurring collections are different instructions, even with the same amount and the same debtor.

Why?

Sequence and mandate state decide which scheme data the collection carries and how the debtor bank treats it. Marking from a guess, or copying last month, processes the collection under the wrong rules.

First or recurring is decided by the mandate, never by a guess.

Why does copying last month's sequence break a first collection?

BA Takeaway

Mark each collection first or recurring from the mandate state, and never copy the sequence from the previous run.

Keep these controls separate:

→ Mandate state, what decides the sequence
→ Sequence flag, first or recurring per collection
→ Scheme data, carried per the sequence

Derive the sequence from the mandate state in the system, and show it on the collection before it is sent.

The real requirement is not "What was the sequence last month?"

It is "What evidence proves this collection carries the right sequence for this mandate?"

Have you seen a collection fail because first and recurring were mixed up?
takeaway: Mark each collection first or recurring from the mandate state, never from a guess.
